newsitem.title: USA: New guidelines issued for colon cancer screening.
newsitem.headline: New guidelines issued for colon cancer screening.

text.p: Everyone should get regular tests for colon cancer from age 50, and people at high risk should consider taking the tests earlier, guidelines issued on Thursday by leading medical groups said.

Colon cancer is second only to lung cancer as the leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States. An estimated 131,000 cases will be diagnosed in the United States alone this year, and nearly 55,000 people will die.

Advanced colon cancer is often fatal but the odds of survival increase dramatically if the cancer is detected early, using screening technology that is now available. Screening can also detect abnormal growths or polyps before they even turn cancerous.

"Colon cancer is one of the most lethal cancers among men and women and is highly preventable," said Dr. Sidney Winawer, co-chairman of the panel of experts who drew up the guidelines and chief of gastroenterology at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre in New York.

"The key is to catch the disease early, before the damage is done, or even detect and remove the premalignant growth that always precedes the cancer and prevent the cancer from developing altogether," he said.
The new guidelines were endorsed by the American Cancer Society, the American College of Gastroenterology and other leading gastroenterology and cancer groups.
The guidelines outline several possible screening methods for people over 50. Some methods can be combined.

One option is annual take-home tests that can detect hidden blood in stool, called fecal occult blood tests. Another is examination of the lower colon for abnormalities through a flexible sigmoidoscope every five years.

Physicians can also do barium enemas with x-rays to study the lower digestive tract every five to 10 years, or a colonoscopy, which permits visualization of the entire colon and removal of any polyps, every 10 years.

More extensive, or earlier, screening is recommended for people with a history of polyps or whose families have a history of colon cancer or a disase called familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Patients with a history of inflammatory bowel disease should also consider earlier screening, the guidelines said.

Most colon cancer occurs in people over age 50 but if someone has a family history of multiple close relatives developing colon cancer at a young age, that person should start screening between the ages of 20 and 30.

Insurance plan coverage varies widely and Medicare does not pay for routine screening, despite past recommendations of various medical groups. But the experts who drew up these guidelines said they are cost-effective.
"Screening for colorectal cancer makes financial sense, said co-chairman Dr. Robert Fletcher, a professor of epidemiology at Harvard Medical School.
